lessons.title: Numbers and types
lessons.summary: Whole numbers, decimals, true/false, and why Rust cares.

cards.p: i32 is a whole number, f64 a decimal, bool is true or false. Rust usually works out the type itself, but you can write it after a colon.
cards.note: i32 means a 32-bit integer and f64 a 64-bit float. Those are the everyday defaults.

cards.p: {} in the text is filled with the next value after the comma. Use it when you want to print a calculation directly.
cards.note: Dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number: the decimal part is dropped. % gives the remainder.

cards.h: Types don't mix on their own

cards.p: Writing let again with the same name makes a new variable that hides the old one. This is called shadowing.
code: let x = x + 1;      // a new x, made from the old one
cards.note: Shadowing is different from mut: each let makes a fresh variable, so it can even have a new type.

cards.p: Every value is owned by one variable. When the owner's block ends at }, the value is cleaned up automatically.

cards.p: &s lends s out without moving it. A function that takes &String can read the text, and the caller keeps it.

cards.h: Box owns a value on the heap
cards.p: Box<T> keeps its value on the heap. The box is its single owner. Use * to read the value. Ordinary local values are fine unless you need this extra indirection.

cards.h: Rc shares ownership on one thread

lessons.title: Steering AI
lessons.summary: Ask for contracts, errors and ownership first; judge the resulting before/after code.

cards.p: Describe what can be represented, not just which sample should print. Ask for type signatures and module boundaries first; review them before requesting the implementation. Here a coordinate always has both components.
cards.note: A types-first request should name illegal states or confused quantities. Do not accept a type merely because its example compiles. crate:: starts a path at the current crate root, so one module can call another module's public function.

cards.p: Ask which layer handles failure and which values are borrowed, moved or copied. Result<T, E> exposes success and failure separately; a typed error can carry useful context. Rc::clone shares an allocation rather than copying its contents.
cards.note: Require an explanation for shared mutation or a clone. Borrowing is not the right answer when the requested value must be independent.

cards.p: u8::MAX and u32::MAX are the largest values of those types. checked_add returns Some(sum), or None on integer overflow. Test failure behavior distinctly from valid zero; a fallback can hide the distinction. assert_eq! checks equality and fails the run if values differ.
cards.note: Use boundary examples the implementation could get wrong. The following tasks ask for contracts and evidence, not a vague promise of idiomatic code.

problems.prompt: Ask: 'Put the shared range rule in one small module and reuse it from both entry points; changing the rule should require one edit.' Which implementation follows that request?
problems.good: Both entry points currently accept the same numbers. The rules module owns one definition; the other implementation separates files conceptually but duplicates the policy, so a future boundary change must be made in two places.
problems.bad: If the rule changes to allow zero, how many definitions must change?

problems.prompt: Ask: 'Return a typed error that callers can match, not a magic sentinel.' Which response?
problems.good: A distinguishes failure from a valid zero. The sample main unwraps known valid input; a real input boundary should match the Result.
problems.bad: Can a caller tell invalid input apart from the number zero?

problems.prompt: Ask: 'Test empty input and a nonempty list where every value is negative, to catch a maximum accidentally initialized to zero.' (`.max()` gives the biggest item of an iterator as an Option; None when it is empty.) Which suite exercises both named edge cases?
problems.good: Both suites test empty and nonempty input. Only [-5, -2] is all-negative, so an incorrect zero starting maximum would fail it; the mixed [-5, 0] case would still pass. This is a named edge-case review, not another ownership signature drill.
problems.bad: Does the supposed negative test actually exclude zero?

problems.prompt: Ask: 'Separate calculation from printing so I can test it without capturing stdout.' Which response?
problems.good: B returns a value from the pure core; main owns printing. Tests can assert sum(&[2,3]) == 5 directly.
problems.bad: Which calculation function exposes its result to a test?

problems.prompt: Ask: 'Return an independent snapshot of shared mutable text, so later edits do not change the saved value.' Which response meets that contract?
problems.good: Cloning the inner String creates independent contents. Rc::clone only adds an owner of the same RefCell. Both show oak initially; a later source.borrow_mut().push would change the shared-clone result too.
problems.bad: Which clone duplicates text, and which only shares its owner?

problems.prompt: Ask: 'Expose only the double operation from this module; callers must not be able to set the multiplier.' Which response keeps that public boundary?
problems.good: Keeping scale private exposes the requested operation without exposing an arbitrary factor. Both versions compute double identically; the distinction is what external callers can request.
problems.bad: Inspect pub on each function, not just the main call.

problems.prompt: Ask: 'Do not overflow at the boundary; return None when addition is impossible.' Which response?
problems.good: B returns None at u32::MAX. A wraps or panics depending on build settings. Ask for a boundary test; the sample 4 cannot distinguish them.
problems.bad: Which operation defines overflow explicitly?

problems.prompt: Ask: 'Write tests that distinguish invalid input from valid zero, even if the parser regresses to returning Ok(0) on errors.' Which test suite catches that regression?
problems.good: The exact Err assertion fails if the parser silently returns Ok(0). The fallback assertion exercises invalid input but collapses both outcomes to zero, so that regression passes. Both suites also test valid zero.
problems.bad: Would replacing the error branch with Ok(0) make either test fail?
